extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, journalism students, and news professionals interested in news production and press sociology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting standards and evaluative dimensions for newsrooms, news content, and journalistic practice (audience relevance, editorial independence, source use, comprehensibility, balance, etc.). Intended for scholars and practitioners analyzing or improving news production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest versus importance (two dimensions of news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between how interesting news is to audiences and how important they consider it; both interest and importance are separate evaluative dimensions of news content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites surveys showing sometimes national news rates higher on importance while local news can rate higher on interest; implies that news selection and presentation should account for both dimensions rather than treating them interchangeably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensibility and clarity of content
rubrics_metrics.description: News and audience mail (letters) should be judged for comprehensibility based on content; unclear grammar or unintelligible writing should be excluded when assessing understandability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes judgments about comprehensibility ‘were based purely on content’ and excluded letters difficult to understand because of poor grammar. Implies evaluation should separate content clarity from surface grammar issues when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and representation of letters/feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors of letters departments choose the most interesting and articulate letters for publication and, when overwhelmed by quantity, lead with particularly emphatic or indignant letters to convey tone and volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: use form letters for routine responses; when a story attracts many letters, select exemplars that reflect both tone and amount of mail—this is an editorial choice about representativeness and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience engagement as indicator of journalist–audience connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Level and character of audience feedback (including strong, repeated reactions) measure the journalists' perceived connection to their audience; even idiosyncratic feedback can be valuable when journalists feel isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote of the recurring ‘mystery lady’ suggests editors may welcome any consistent audience response as evidence of connection; be wary that such feedback may not represent wider audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining and targeting audience segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and news organizations should identify and distinguish among audience subgroups (e.g., lay readers, professionals, 'policy players' vs. 'policy makers') and tailor content/tones accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: back-of-book writers develop dichotomous images (professional vs lay); Washington Post reporters distinguish policy players and policy makers—audience conception affects news selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and resistance to external pressure (anti-censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should resist external pressures (advertisers, sponsors, affiliates, government, owners) that lead to killing, altering, or softening stories; censorship is treated as externally demanded suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines censorship from news-organization perspective (external demand). Numerous examples: advertiser withdrawal allegedly killed Life expose; sponsor pressure altered NBC documentary; affiliate and White House pressures on broadcasts. Anti-pattern: yielding to advertiser/owner/affiliate pressure to avoid financial or political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship and organizational restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' own or organizationally-induced restraint (self-censorship, transfers, suppression of reporting) undermines reporting; evaluators should look for institutional constraints that mute reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include transfers or removal of reporters after management/affiliate pressure and the practice of editors changing copy—distinguish external censorship from internal editorial changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality in crime coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of crime news should bear some relation to actual crime rates to avoid exaggerated public perception of crime prevalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation (Jones): where journalists emphasize dramatic crimes, they can 'tag' stories by reporting actual crime rates to provide balance and context and counteract exaggeration from highlighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiperspectival reporting balanced with intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide multiple perspectives in news coverage, but be aware that excessive conflicting perspectives can make 'objectivity' function merely as a detached yardstick rather than informative context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites the risk that when too many conflicting perspectives appear, objectivity can become a 'yardstick of reality' credible solely for detachment—implies balancing plurality with coherent, comprehensible framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and use of sources (source power and representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess sources as roles and representatives of organized/unorganized groups, examine who gets access to news, the agendas they pursue, and the power implications of source selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers (and newsrooms) should determine what groups create or become sources, why some groups cannot get into the news, and the effects on groups' subsequent power and activities when they do or do not obtain access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible language across audience strata
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should use language that is understandable to ordinary audiences (e.g., 'talk to be understood by the truck driver') without 'insulting the professor's intelligence'—i.e., clear but not condescending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ed Murrow's principle encourages balancing simplicity and sophistication in presentation; applicable to both spoken and written news forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor and statistical literacy (precision journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should be persuaded of and trained in the relevance of statistics and sampling theory to improve reporting accuracy and representativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to Philip Meyer's 'Precision Journalism' as an attempt to introduce statistical methods to journalists—encourages use of empirical methods rather than solely anecdotal impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about journalistic materials (outtakes, notes) when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: When legally or publicly relevant, journalists and producers may be required to disclose notes, outtakes, or thinking behind a story; transparency is an evaluative criterion for accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes a Supreme Court case considering whether a producer must disclose thoughts and opinions held in preparing a program segment—implies tradeoffs between source/producers' privacy and public accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding undue concentration/monopoly and increasing citizen access
rubrics_metrics.description: Media-reform aims (reduce cross-ownership monopolies, increase public-service programming, increase citizen access to local media) are normative criteria for a healthier news environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movement examples (United Church of Christ, Nader org, public-interest law firms) seek democratization of media ownership and participation; evaluators should factor structural media ownership and access into assessments of newsroom performance and public service.
